lines: Everything up to here treated a flow of events as just that: a flow, one event after another.
There's a completely different, equally valid way of looking at that same exact thing.
What does seeing it that other way actually end up buying anyone?
Everything covered so far sat underneath whatever particular way someone happened to be interacting with it.
This part is the layer most people actually spend their time working in directly.
Describing what should happen, declaratively, over something that keeps on changing.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A flow of new things and changed things gets read as one single changing table instead.
If that had to turn back into a flow of changes again, how many genuinely different ways could one single change get written down?
answer: A handful of genuinely different ways, each with its own real trade-offs.
One way only ever adds. Another one replaces, by some fixed identity. A third one pairs an undo with a redo.
None of them is simply the correct one. Each one trades something away for something else.

lines: One way only ever adds something new, never replacing or undoing anything that came before.
A different way replaces whatever already carried the same identity, outright.
A third way writes down an explicit undo of the old thing, paired with a redo of the new one.
Replacing by identity needs that identity to actually exist and be unique in the first place.
Pairing an undo with a redo needs no such identity at all, but it isn't free either.
One single change costs twice as much to write down, every single time, under that second approach.
One way of matching two flows against each other assumes absolutely anything could still match absolutely anything else, later.
Because of that assumption, it has to hang onto everything it has ever seen from both sides.
Nothing it's holding onto ever gets to be safely thrown away, not ever.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
Suppose matching two flows only ever needs things that showed up close together in time.
What happens, then, to everything that approach has to keep hanging onto?
answer: What gets kept hanging onto stops growing without limit, and here's why.
The moment something falls outside that close window, it simply can't ever match anything again.
So it becomes safe to just let it go, unlike the version that assumed anything could match anything.

lines: One way of bounding what gets kept uses an actual window of real time on both sides.
A different way bounds it in a completely different manner altogether.
It matches against whichever version was current back then, and keeps no window at all, just that one current version.
One further way skips keeping its own side at all, and instead reaches outward every single time.
An even newer way goes one step further than that, reusing what the source already holds directly.
Instead of duplicating any of it into something kept separately on the side.
A separate kind of table defines its own refresh, driven entirely by how fresh it was asked to stay.
Ask for something close to fresh, and a continuously running process keeps it that way.
Ask for something far looser, and a process that only triggers now and then is enough instead.
Every number in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy model.
The handful of ways of writing down a change that really did cost genuinely different amounts.
One matching approach that really did keep growing, right beside another one that really did level off.
So: the same exact changing thing, written down in more than one genuinely different way.
Every single way of matching two flows is really just a different answer to one question.
How much does it actually have to hang onto. Everything layered on top sits above all of that, never underneath it.
